name: Black cohosh
short: Case reports link black cohosh to liver injury, including liver failure needing transplant and death; causality is often uncertain, and pooled trials of one extract found no liver-enzyme changes.
text: A systematic review of adverse events identified 13 clinical trials, all of which indicated relative safety, together with 3 postmarketing surveillance studies, 4 case series and 8 single case reports; it judged that causal attribution was problematic in most case reports, yet concluded that black cohosh has been associated with serious safety concerns that urgently require further investigation. The serious concern is liver injury, and the evidence for it is case reports: one describes a 60-year-old woman with subacute liver failure attributed to black cohosh who went on to liver transplantation, which its authors counted as the fifth such reported case, and they recommended monitoring of liver function in people taking it. A 2025 review states that many case studies document outcomes ranging from mild reactions to acute liver damage and even death, and that recent studies indicate black cohosh extract induces genotoxicity; the abstract does not say whether those genotoxicity studies were in people, and the review covers in vivo and in vitro experiments as well as clinical trials. It also notes that commercial products can differ markedly in composition. In contrast, a meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials of one specific (isopropanolic) extract in 1,117 women treated for 3 to 6 months found no significant effect on the liver enzymes AST or ALT and no evidence of an adverse effect on liver function. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
